content: The primary impact of influenza in children and adults is absenteeism from school and work. However, children and individuals over 65 years of age are at the highest risk for complications. This review, an update of a 2011 publication, evaluates the efficacy, effectiveness, and potential harms of influenza vaccines in healthy children. Future updates will only occur if new trials or vaccines become available. Observational data from previous versions of the review have been retained for historical context but are no longer updated due to their limited influence on the conclusions. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing influenza vaccines to placebo or no intervention in children under 16 years of age. Observational studies, such as cohort and case-control studies, were included in earlier versions but are no longer updated. The authors independently assessed the risk of bias and extracted data, using the GRADE system to evaluate the certainty of evidence for key outcomes, including influenza, influenza-like illness (ILI), complications (e.g., hospitalization, ear infections), and adverse events. Absolute effects were reported based on median control group risks, and numbers needed to vaccinate (NNVs) were calculated accordingly. A total of 41 clinical trials involving over 200,000 children were included. Most studies focused on children older than two years and compared live attenuated or inactivated vaccines to placebo or no vaccine. These trials were conducted across various regions, including the USA, Western Europe, Russia, and Bangladesh, between 1984 and 2013. Analyses restricted to studies with a low risk of bias showed that influenza and otitis media were the only outcomes minimally affected by bias. Variability in study design and reporting limited the ability to perform meta-analyses for adverse events. Live Attenuated Vaccines In children aged 3 to 16 years, live attenuated influenza vaccines likely reduce the risk of influenza infection from 18% to 4% (risk ratio [RR] 0.22, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.11 to 0.41; moderate-certainty evidence). These vaccines may also reduce the risk of ILI from 17% to 12% (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.80; low-certainty evidence). To prevent one case of influenza, seven children would need to be vaccinated, and to prevent one case of ILI, 20 children would need to be vaccinated. The risk of acute otitis media appears similar between vaccinated and unvaccinated children during seasonal influenza, based on a single study with high rates of otitis media (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.01; moderate-certainty evidence). There is insufficient evidence to determine the effect of vaccination on school absenteeism due to very low-certainty evidence from one study. Vaccination may reduce the need for parents to take time off work, but the confidence interval includes no effect (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.46 to 1.03; low-certainty evidence). Data on severe complications, such as hospitalizations, were not available. Fever following vaccination varied widely, ranging from 0.16% to 15% in children receiving live vaccines, compared to 0.71% to 22% in placebo groups (very low-certainty evidence). Data on nausea were not reported. Inactivated Vaccines In children aged 2 to 16 years, inactivated vaccines reduce the risk of influenza from 30% to 11% (RR 0.36, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.48; high-certainty evidence). These vaccines likely reduce the risk of ILI from 28% to 20% (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.79; moderate-certainty evidence). To prevent one case of influenza, five children would need to be vaccinated, and to prevent one case of ILI, 12 children would need to be vaccinated. The risk of otitis media is likely similar between vaccinated and unvaccinated children (31% versus 27%), although the confidence interval does not exclude a potential increase in otitis media following vaccination (RR 1.15, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.40; moderate-certainty evidence). There is insufficient evidence to determine the effect of vaccination on school absenteeism due to very low-certainty evidence from one study. No data were available on parental working time lost, hospitalizations, fever, or nausea. Limited evidence was found on secondary cases, treatment for lower respiratory tract disease, and drug prescriptions. One monovalent pandemic vaccine was associated with rare but serious adverse events, including cataplexy (sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by intense emotions) and narcolepsy (a sleep disorder) in children. Evidence of other serious harms, such as febrile seizures, was sparse. Authors' Conclusions In children aged 3 to 16 years, live attenuated influenza vaccines likely reduce the risk of influenza (moderate-certainty evidence) and may reduce the risk of ILI (low-certainty evidence) during a single influenza season. Inactivated vaccines reduce the risk of influenza (high-certainty evidence) and may reduce the risk of ILI (low-certainty evidence) in the same population. However, the absolute reduction in influenza and ILI varied significantly across study populations, making it challenging to generalize these findings to different settings. Few RCTs were conducted in children under two years of age, and adverse event data were poorly described in the available studies. Standardized methods for defining, identifying, and reporting adverse events are needed. Identifying all global cases of potential harms was beyond the scope of this review.
